title: Categorical logic and syllogisms
note: Categorical statements relate two classes: A 'All S are P', E 'No S are P', I 'Some S are P', O 'Some S are not P'. A and O are contradictories, as are E and I. A syllogism has three terms: the major term (predicate of the conclusion), the minor term (subject of the conclusion), and the middle term, which appears in both premises but not the conclusion.

read.title: The square of opposition
text: Categorical logic, begun by Aristotle, studies statements that relate two classes. There are four standard forms. A: All S are P. E: No S are P. I: Some S are P. O: Some S are not P. A and E are universal, I and O particular; A and I are affirmative, E and O negative.

The square of opposition maps their logical relations. A and O are contradictories, as are E and I: exactly one of each pair is true. 'All dogs bark' is false precisely when some dog does not bark. On the traditional square, A and E are contraries, which cannot both be true but can both be false, while I and O are subcontraries, which cannot both be false. Truth also flows downward: if all S are P, then some S are P.

Modern logic reads universal statements differently. 'All unicorns have horns' is treated as 'anything that is a unicorn has a horn', which is true if there are no unicorns at all. On this Boolean reading only I and O imply that something exists, so the downward inference fails, and only the contradictory relations survive.
Venn diagrams test these claims: shade a region to mark it empty, and place an X to mark that something is there.

q.q: On any reading, what is the relation between 'All dogs bark' and 'Some dogs do not bark'?
Why does the downward inference from A to I fail on the Boolean reading?
o: Universal statements do not imply that their subjects exist
